title: Fruit worthy of repentance (Matthew 3:1–12)
hookLine: don't rely on your ancestors; bear fruit
tomorrow: why would Jesus get in line for something he didn't need?

cards: Public apologies have their own look now: the soft lighting, the notes-app statement, the line about doing a lot of reflecting. And the comments ask: but what changes? A man at the Jordan River asked that long before.

John the Baptist, in camel's hair and a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, preaching: "Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Crowds come out, confess their sins, and go down into the river.
Then a group of leaders arrives.

teach.b: John sees Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, leaders of his own people, and he doesn't soften it.
He's a prophet speaking hard to his own family, not a stranger judging from outside: "Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance." Meet is old English for fitting.
And he shuts a shortcut: "think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father." A family tree won't stand in for a life. So what is repentance?
Christians answer two ways, and both start on this riverbank.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: A MOMENT AT THE RIVER.
teach.b: The first view says it's a moment. Look at the crowd: they walk into the water, confess, and come up turned around. A turning has a day and a place, and some churches mark it with a baptism or a call to come forward.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: A WHOLE LIFE OF TURNING.
teach.b: The second view says it's a whole life. Martin Luther's first thesis says that when Jesus said repent, he meant the whole life of believers to be repentance.
A tree doesn't bear fruit once; it bears it season after season. The first view answers: every tree is planted on one day. The second answers: and then it keeps growing.
On John's point, the two agree: a turning nobody can see isn't the kind he asked for.

how: Some churches read John the Baptist's preaching in Advent, and in confession or a time of examination some Christians ask not only what they're sorry for but what they will do differently.

games.q: what does “fruit worthy of repentance” mean?
o: a shame that lingers long after a mistake
a change of heart you can see in actions
a punishment handed out for a wrong done

games.q: fruit worthy of repentance — tap the pairs.
p: camel's hair and a leather belt
an old word for fitting, worthy
we have Abraham to our father
what John says not to lean on

s: for John, repentance is mainly a feeling of being very sorry
he asks for fruit: a turning that shows in what you do.
John told the leaders their family tree would keep them safe
think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father.
John lived on locusts and wild honey
Matthew describes his camel's-hair coat, leather belt, and that food.

games.q: you've always pictured repenting as one big moment, at a river or an altar. state the whole-life view at its strongest.
o: a tree bears fruit season after season; Luther's first thesis calls the whole life repentance.
the moment at the river is fake, so it should be skipped.
repentance only counts if you cry, since tears prove you mean it.
games.why: the whole-life view keeps the moment and adds the seasons. the moment view replies that every tree is planted on one day. both stand with John: the turning has to show.

practice: Choose one change you've meant to make, and do the smallest real piece of it before the sit ends: move the phone to another room, delete the version you shouldn't send, set out the shoes for the walk you keep skipping.
Then sit back down with that one piece of fruit already on the branch.

wordCard.voice: Fruit worthy of repentance. John's call for a turning that shows, not a family tree to lean on.

orig.note: Greek: repentance, a turning. the word behind repentance in Matthew 3:8.

carryVoice: Your line: bear fruit. A moment or a lifetime, the change has to show. See you tomorrow.
